title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 55
paragraphs: These lines, when they reached him, pleased Croesus more than all the rest, for he supposed that a mule would never be ruler of the Medes in place of a man, and that consequently he himself and his heirs would never cease from their rule. After this he turned his thoughts to inquiring which of the Greek peoples he should esteem the most powerful and win over to himself as friends. On inquiring he found that the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians had the pre-eminence, the first among the Dorian and the others among the Ionian race. For these were the most eminent peoples in ancient times, the second being a Pelasgian and the first a Hellenic race. The one never migrated from its original seat in any direction, while the other was exceedingly given to wanderings. For in the reign of Deucalion this race dwelt in Phthiotis, and in the time of Dorus, son of Hellen, in the land lying below Ossa and Olympus, which is called Histiaeotis. When it was driven out of Histiaeotis by the sons of Cadmus, it dwelt in Pindus and was called Macednian; from there it moved afterward to Dryopis, and from Dryopis it came finally to the Peloponnesus, where it began to be called Dorian.
